cards.front: What does the compiler generate for an enum?
cards.back: A class extending java.lang.Enum, with one instance per constant
cards.extra: Enums are real classes: they can have fields, constructors and methods. That is why they can do far more than a list of ints.

cards.back: An array of the constants in declaration order
cards.extra: It is generated by the compiler, not inherited. The array is a copy, so mutating it does not affect the enum.

cards.front: What does ordinal() return, and why is it risky?
cards.back: The declaration index starting at 0 — risky because reordering constants silently changes persisted data
cards.extra: Never store ordinals in a database or file. Store name() and read it back with valueOf.

cards.front: Is == safe for comparing enum constants?
cards.back: Yes — each constant is a single instance, so identity and equality coincide
cards.extra: No override of equals is needed or wanted. That makes switch on an enum both safe and readable.

cards.front: What does Enum.valueOf(Foo.class, "BAR") do when the name is unknown?
cards.extra: It does not return null, so untrusted input needs a try/catch or a values() scan. Guessing here is how bad config crashes a service.

cards.front: Can an enum have methods and constructors?
cards.back: Yes — constructors are implicitly private and run once per constant
cards.extra: That is how a constant carries extra data: MONDAY(1) stores its own field. Constants can even override methods individually.

cards.front: What replaces a set of boolean or bit flags?
cards.back: EnumSet — a set backed by a bit vector, fast and type-safe
cards.extra: It is as cheap as flags but cannot hold a value outside the enum, and it iterates in declaration order.
